evals.name: dependency-unlock
evals.prompt: Recommend the next slice. Materials are in evals/next-best-slice/cases/case-001/: review.md, retro.md, backlog.md.
evals.expected_output: Recommends protecting /api/account with the new require_auth decorator: small, directly builds on the capability the retro says now exists for the first time, fixes a real access-control gap (any caller can currently read any account's details), and is a genuine dependency unlock rather than a preference call. The RBAC system and routing refactor both wait as too large / not evidence-justified yet.
expectations: The Recommendation is the /api/account protection slice (applying require_auth and reading the user id from the verified token), not the RBAC system, the routing refactor, or rate limiting
Why now explicitly ties the recommendation to the architectural consequence named in retro.md (any route can now require auth via one decorator) rather than to general priority or preference
Alternatives considered explains why the RBAC system and the routing refactor wait — evidence-grounded reasons (too large / not justified by anything in the review or retro), not just 'not now'

evals.name: user-value-vs-prerequisite
evals.prompt: Recommend the next slice. Materials are in evals/next-best-slice/cases/case-002/: review.md, retro.md, backlog.md.
evals.expected_output: A genuine judgment call between two defensible picks: swapping to an indexed search backend (addresses the review-flagged, non-hypothetical growth risk: 380ms on 500 rows vs. a 118k-row and growing production catalog) or instrumenting production search latency first (the smallest way to get a real number before committing to the swap). Either is acceptable if the reasoning explicitly engages with the flagged scale numbers using the skill's own criteria. What's not acceptable: picking a pure UI feature (highlighting/filters) while ignoring the scale risk entirely, or jumping to a bigger initiative than an indexed-search swap (e.g. a full search-platform migration).
expectations: The Recommendation is either the FTS5/indexed-search swap or the production-latency-instrumentation slice -- not the highlighting or filters candidates, and not an oversized rewrite/migration beyond a bounded swap

Why now explicitly cites the specific numbers from review.md/retro.md (380ms on the 500-row fixture, ~118,000-row and growing production catalog) rather than a generic 'search should be fast' justification

The response explicitly weighs the chosen candidate against the other defensible one (indexed-search swap vs. instrumentation) using criteria like size, reversibility, or risk reduction, rather than picking one without acknowledging the other was a real option

evals.name: equally-attractive-candidates
evals.prompt: Recommend the next slice. Materials are in evals/next-best-slice/cases/case-003/: review.md, retro.md, backlog.md.
evals.expected_output: All three notification channels (email, SMS, push) are genuinely close in value and size. A good recommendation picks exactly one -- email or push are the more defensible picks since both reuse existing infrastructure (SMTP creds already exist; push tokens are already registered), while SMS requires provisioning a brand-new external vendor account -- and states the tiebreak plainly rather than implying the choice was more obvious than it is. Recommending more than one channel, or a phased multi-channel plan, fails regardless of which channel is picked.
expectations: Exactly one channel is recommended (email, SMS, or push) -- not two, not all three, not a sequenced/phased list of channels

The recommendation names a concrete, evidence-grounded tiebreak (e.g. reuses existing SMTP credentials, or reuses existing push-token infrastructure) rather than presenting the choice as though it were the only reasonable option
Alternatives considered explicitly acknowledges the other channel(s) were close calls rather than dismissing them as obviously wrong

evals.name: narrow-experiment-vs-milestone
evals.prompt: Recommend the next slice. Materials are in evals/next-best-slice/cases/case-004/: review.md, retro.md, backlog.md.
evals.expected_output: Recommends the bounded 500-SKU A/B test with real conversion tracking, not the full ~118,000-SKU catalog rollout. The retro's evidence (two editors' unscored, unblinded impression) is far too thin to justify replacing real copy site-wide, and a full rollout is much harder to reverse. The A/B test is sized specifically to answer the retro's own open question (does this move a real metric) before any larger commitment.
expectations: The Recommendation is the bounded 500-SKU A/B test, not the full-catalog rollout, the regenerate-button feature, or the additional-languages feature

Why now / Why they wait explicitly identifies that the full rollout is not justified by the current evidence (an informal, unscored editor read-through is not a customer-behavior measurement) and is harder to reverse once shipped site-wide
What this slice proves is framed around settling the retro's actual open question (whether AI copy moves a real business metric), not around shipping AI descriptions as a feature in itself

evals.name: deferred-not-yet-justified
evals.prompt: Recommend the next slice. Materials are in evals/next-best-slice/cases/case-005/: review.md, retro.md, backlog.md.
evals.expected_output: Does not recommend building the Redis-backed distributed rate limiter: it was deferred for a specific infrastructure reason (Redis not provisioned) that nothing in this evidence shows has changed, and nothing shows the per-instance gap is actually being exploited. The justified next step is the small rejection-metric slice, which would produce the evidence needed to know whether the deferred work is actually needed.
expectations: The Recommendation is not the Redis-backed distributed rate limiter -- the response recognizes it's still not justified by anything in review.md or retro.md

The response explains specifically why the Redis limiter isn't yet justified: it was deferred for an infrastructure reason (Redis unavailable) that this evidence doesn't show has changed, not just 'let's not do the big thing'

The Recommendation is the rejection-metric/logging slice (or an equivalently small evidence-producing slice) rather than the allowlist or admin-dashboard candidates, which don't address the open cross-instance question at all

evals.name: evidence-changes-direction
evals.prompt: Recommend the next slice. Materials are in evals/next-best-slice/cases/case-006/: review.md, retro.md, backlog.md.
evals.expected_output: Recommends increasing the cache capacity from 128 to 2048 entries and re-measuring against the same p95/hit-rate benchmark -- the smallest, cheapest way to test one of the three hypotheses the retro's falsified assumption raised (sizing vs. key-space vs. not-cacheable), rather than jumping straight to a bigger commitment (a shared Redis cache prototype) or continuing to invest in the original, now-falsified direction (cache warming, rolling the same approach out to more endpoints) without first learning why hit rate is low.
expectations: The Recommendation is the capacity-increase-and-remeasure slice, not cache warming, not rolling the pattern out to 6 other endpoints, and not (as the primary pick) the shared Redis cache prototype
Why now explicitly ties back to the falsified assumption in retro.md (in-process caching alone did not meet the 50ms target) and to the specific open hypotheses retro.md's follow-up question raises

The response explains why rolling the same in-process-cache pattern out to more endpoints is premature given the falsified assumption -- it doesn't treat this slice's cache approach as already proven successful

evals.name: gather-more-evidence
evals.prompt: Recommend the next slice. Materials are in evals/next-best-slice/cases/case-007/: review.md, retro.md, backlog.md.
evals.expected_output: Recommends extending the canary (larger sample and/or longer window, sized to reach statistical significance) rather than rolling out to 100% or rolling back entirely. Both of those are premature commitments given data eng's own statement that the current error-rate delta is noise, not a real signal. The satisfaction-survey candidate is a plausible-sounding distraction that doesn't address the actual open question.
expectations: The Recommendation is to extend the canary (larger sample and/or longer duration, sized to reach significance) rather than a full rollout, a full rollback, or the satisfaction-survey candidate

The response explicitly states that neither rollout nor rollback is currently justified, citing data eng's own statement that the 1.28% vs 1.39% delta is within normal noise for this sample size -- it does not treat the delta as either a validated or falsified safety claim
What this slice proves is framed as answering the open statistical question (is the new flow's error rate actually different), not as a feature or UX improvement
